raw_evidence.label: MedDRA: the shared vocabulary behind every reaction term
raw_evidence.content: Every reaction in FAERS is recorded as a MedDRA Preferred Term, a standardized medical vocabulary used by drug regulators and the pharmaceutical industry worldwide. MedDRA is hierarchical: Preferred Terms (e.g. 'Nausea', 'Drug ineffective') aggregate into System Organ Classes (e.g. 'Nervous system disorders', 'Vascular disorders'). For the FAERS reader this matters because reaction language is not free text — when 'Drug ineffective' shows up thousands of times, it is exactly the same code each time, and the same vocabulary is used by EU and Japanese regulators. This makes cross-drug and cross-country comparison clean, but it also funnels disparate clinical experiences into a finite list of terms.

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

raw_evidence.label: The top 'reaction' isn't medical — it's 'Off label use'
raw_evidence.content: Of 597,802 reaction rows, the single most common MedDRA Preferred Term is 'Off label use' (14,801 mentions, 2.48%), followed by 'Drug ineffective' (11,335, 1.90%) and 'Death' (9,356, 1.57%). Only at rank four does a recognisably medical symptom appear: 'Fatigue' (8,170, 1.37%). The top ten is heavy with terms that describe how the drug was used or whether it worked, not what happened to the patient: 'Off label use', 'Drug ineffective', 'Product dose omission issue', 'Drug dose omission by device'. This is structural: FAERS reports are filed by anyone who notices a problem, and many manufacturer-mandated reports are triggered by complaints that a drug failed to work or was used outside its label — not by a physical adverse event.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_12: Top 30 MedDRA Preferred Terms ---
print("=== ana_12 ===")
top_pt = reactions["reactionmeddrapt"].value_counts().head(30)
total_react_rows = len(reactions)
for pt, n in top_pt.items():
    print(f"{pt}\t{n:,}\t{n/total_react_rows*100:.2f}%")
print(f"total reaction rows: {total_react_rows:,}")
print(f"unique PT terms: {reactions['reactionmeddrapt'].nunique():,}")

raw_evidence.label: MedDRA: the shared vocabulary behind every reaction term
raw_evidence.content: Every reaction in FAERS is recorded as a MedDRA Preferred Term, a standardized medical vocabulary used by drug regulators and the pharmaceutical industry worldwide. MedDRA is hierarchical: Preferred Terms (e.g. 'Nausea', 'Drug ineffective') aggregate into System Organ Classes (e.g. 'Nervous system disorders', 'Vascular disorders'). For the FAERS reader this matters because reaction language is not free text — when 'Drug ineffective' shows up thousands of times, it is exactly the same code each time, and the same vocabulary is used by EU and Japanese regulators. This makes cross-drug and cross-country comparison clean, but it also funnels disparate clinical experiences into a finite list of terms.

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

raw_evidence.label: What FAERS is and where this data comes from
raw_evidence.content: The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) is the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's central database for post-market drug safety reports. It collects voluntary reports from patients, caregivers, and clinicians via MedWatch, plus mandatory expedited reports from drug manufacturers. The system supports the FDA's post-market safety surveillance for drugs and therapeutic biologics. FAERS data is published quarterly and exposed via the OpenFDA Drug Adverse Event API at https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json. This blog uses a roughly chronological API-paginated sample of 200,000 reports with receivedate in 2024, drawn from a full-year universe of approximately 1.32 million reports.

raw_evidence.label: How a FAERS report is structured
raw_evidence.content: Each FAERS record describes one adverse-event report. A report names one patient (age, sex, country), one or more drugs (each tagged as Suspect, Concomitant, or Interacting in the drugcharacterization field), and one or more reactions described as standardized MedDRA Preferred Terms. The report carries a single seriousness flag (`serious`: 1=serious, 2=not serious) and sub-flags for death and hospitalization. The reporter is classified by `reporttype` — 1=Spontaneous (the typical MedWatch submission), 2=Report from study, 3=Other, 4=Not available to sender. A single safetyreportid therefore explodes into many rows: one summary row, n_drugs drug rows, and n_reactions reaction rows.

raw_evidence.label: Sampling caveat for this 200k slice of 2024
raw_evidence.content: The dataset in front of us is not the full FAERS 2024 universe of ~1.32 million reports. It is a 200,000-report sample, drawn chronologically through ~4-day windows of the OpenFDA API and deduplicated by safetyreportid. That means: (a) every receivedate in 2024 is represented in proportion to its API ordering, not in proportion to true volume, so monthly totals should be read as 'reports captured in our sample' rather than 'monthly FAERS volume'; (b) drugs with very long-tail counts (rare-disease therapies, recent launches) may be sparsely represented; and (c) the per-row fields are themselves a flattened summary of OpenFDA's nested JSON — secondary suspect drugs, dose, and concomitant medications other than the first few are not included. The dataset is large enough for solid relative analyses (which drugs dominate, which reactions cluster, demographic skew) and weak for rate estimation (how often does X happen per prescription).

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates

raw_evidence.label: Missing-data profile of the summary table

raw_evidence.label: 52% of reports are tagged 'serious'; 9% record a death
raw_evidence.content: The serious flag is on in 104,896 of 200,000 reports (52.5%). Of those, 18,865 reports (9.4% of all 200,000) carry the seriousnessdeath sub-flag, and 38,124 (19.1%) carry the seriousnesshospitalization sub-flag. The 'serious' rate is much higher than naive expectation because serious events are far more likely to be reported in the first place — a mild headache rarely makes it into FAERS, but a hospitalization almost always does. The 9.4% death rate is therefore not 'how often this drug kills' but 'what share of reports involve a death'.

# --- ana_18: Overall seriousness rates ---
print("=== ana_18 ===")
N = len(sample)
serious_n = (sample["serious"] == 1).sum()
notser_n  = (sample["serious"] == 2).sum()
death_n   = (sample["seriousnessdeath"] == 1).sum()
hosp_n    = (sample["seriousnesshospitalization"] == 1).sum()
print(f"total reports: {N:,}")
print(f"serious=1: {serious_n:,} ({serious_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"serious=2 (not serious): {notser_n:,} ({notser_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"seriousnessdeath=1: {death_n:,} ({death_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"seriousnesshospitalization=1: {hosp_n:,} ({hosp_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"death OR hospitalization: {((sample['seriousnessdeath']==1)|(sample['seriousnesshospitalization']==1)).sum():,}")

raw_evidence.label: Encoding correction: '2' means 'no', not 'blank'
raw_evidence.content: The README says seriousnessdeath and seriousnesshospitalization are coded 1=true and blank=false. The actual data encodes them as 1=true, 2=false, and NaN=missing. seriousnessdeath has 18,865 ones (9.4%), 172,924 twos (86.5%), and 8,211 missing values. Without correcting this, every chart that filters on `seriousnessdeath != null` would overcount deaths fourteen-fold. Every seriousness statistic in this analysis uses the value 1 as the positive class.

raw_evidence.label: What FAERS is and where this data comes from
raw_evidence.content: The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) is the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's central database for post-market drug safety reports. It collects voluntary reports from patients, caregivers, and clinicians via MedWatch, plus mandatory expedited reports from drug manufacturers. The system supports the FDA's post-market safety surveillance for drugs and therapeutic biologics. FAERS data is published quarterly and exposed via the OpenFDA Drug Adverse Event API at https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json. This blog uses a roughly chronological API-paginated sample of 200,000 reports with receivedate in 2024, drawn from a full-year universe of approximately 1.32 million reports.

raw_evidence.label: How a FAERS report is structured
raw_evidence.content: Each FAERS record describes one adverse-event report. A report names one patient (age, sex, country), one or more drugs (each tagged as Suspect, Concomitant, or Interacting in the drugcharacterization field), and one or more reactions described as standardized MedDRA Preferred Terms. The report carries a single seriousness flag (`serious`: 1=serious, 2=not serious) and sub-flags for death and hospitalization. The reporter is classified by `reporttype` — 1=Spontaneous (the typical MedWatch submission), 2=Report from study, 3=Other, 4=Not available to sender. A single safetyreportid therefore explodes into many rows: one summary row, n_drugs drug rows, and n_reactions reaction rows.

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

raw_evidence.label: 52% of reports are tagged 'serious'; 9% record a death
raw_evidence.content: The serious flag is on in 104,896 of 200,000 reports (52.5%). Of those, 18,865 reports (9.4% of all 200,000) carry the seriousnessdeath sub-flag, and 38,124 (19.1%) carry the seriousnesshospitalization sub-flag. The 'serious' rate is much higher than naive expectation because serious events are far more likely to be reported in the first place — a mild headache rarely makes it into FAERS, but a hospitalization almost always does. The 9.4% death rate is therefore not 'how often this drug kills' but 'what share of reports involve a death'.

raw_evidence.label: How a FAERS report is structured
raw_evidence.content: Each FAERS record describes one adverse-event report. A report names one patient (age, sex, country), one or more drugs (each tagged as Suspect, Concomitant, or Interacting in the drugcharacterization field), and one or more reactions described as standardized MedDRA Preferred Terms. The report carries a single seriousness flag (`serious`: 1=serious, 2=not serious) and sub-flags for death and hospitalization. raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

raw_evidence.label: What FAERS is and where this data comes from
raw_evidence.content: The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) is the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's central database for post-market drug safety reports. It collects voluntary reports from patients, caregivers, and clinicians via MedWatch, plus mandatory expedited reports from drug manufacturers. The system supports the FDA's post-market safety surveillance for drugs and therapeutic biologics. FAERS data is published quarterly and exposed via the OpenFDA Drug Adverse Event API at https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json. This blog uses a roughly chronological API-paginated sample of 200,000 reports with receivedate in 2024, drawn from a full-year universe of approximately 1.32 million reports.

raw_evidence.label: How a FAERS report is structured
raw_evidence.content: Each FAERS record describes one adverse-event report. A report names one patient (age, sex, country), one or more drugs (each tagged as Suspect, Concomitant, or Interacting in the drugcharacterization field), and one or more reactions described as standardized MedDRA Preferred Terms. The report carries a single seriousness flag (`serious`: 1=serious, 2=not serious) and sub-flags for death and hospitalization. The reporter is classified by `reporttype` — 1=Spontaneous (the typical MedWatch submission), 2=Report from study, 3=Other, 4=Not available to sender. A single safetyreportid therefore explodes into many rows: one summary row, n_drugs drug rows, and n_reactions reaction rows.

raw_evidence.label: How a FAERS report is structured
raw_evidence.content: Each FAERS record describes one adverse-event report. A report names one patient (age, sex, country), one or more drugs (each tagged as Suspect, Concomitant, or Interacting in the drugcharacterization field), and one or more reactions described as standardized MedDRA Preferred Terms. The report carries a single seriousness flag (`serious`: 1=serious, 2=not serious) and sub-flags for death and hospitalization. The reporter is classified by `reporttype` — 1=Spontaneous (the typical MedWatch submission), 2=Report from study, 3=Other, 4=Not available to sender. A single safetyreportid therefore explodes into many rows: one summary row, n_drugs drug rows, and n_reactions reaction rows.

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

raw_evidence.label: Sampling caveat for this 200k slice of 2024
raw_evidence.content: The dataset in front of us is not the full FAERS 2024 universe of ~1.32 million reports. It is a 200,000-report sample, drawn chronologically through ~4-day windows of the OpenFDA API and deduplicated by safetyreportid. That means: (a) every receivedate in 2024 is represented in proportion to its API ordering, not in proportion to true volume, so monthly totals should be read as 'reports captured in our sample' rather than 'monthly FAERS volume'; (b) drugs with very long-tail counts (rare-disease therapies, recent launches) may be sparsely represented; and (c) the per-row fields are themselves a flattened summary of OpenFDA's nested JSON — secondary suspect drugs, dose, and concomitant medications other than the first few are not included. The dataset is large enough for solid relative analyses (which drugs dominate, which reactions cluster, demographic skew) and weak for rate estimation (how often does X happen per prescription).

raw_evidence.label: 52% of reports are tagged 'serious'; 9% record a death
raw_evidence.content: The serious flag is on in 104,896 of 200,000 reports (52.5%). Of those, 18,865 reports (9.4% of all 200,000) carry the seriousnessdeath sub-flag, and 38,124 (19.1%) carry the seriousnesshospitalization sub-flag. The 'serious' rate is much higher than naive expectation because serious events are far more likely to be reported in the first place — a mild headache rarely makes it into FAERS, but a hospitalization almost always does. The 9.4% death rate is therefore not 'how often this drug kills' but 'what share of reports involve a death'.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_18: Overall seriousness rates ---
print("=== ana_18 ===")
N = len(sample)
serious_n = (sample["serious"] == 1).sum()
notser_n  = (sample["serious"] == 2).sum()
death_n   = (sample["seriousnessdeath"] == 1).sum()
hosp_n    = (sample["seriousnesshospitalization"] == 1).sum()
print(f"total reports: {N:,}")
print(f"serious=1: {serious_n:,} ({serious_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"serious=2 (not serious): {notser_n:,} ({notser_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"seriousnessdeath=1: {death_n:,} ({death_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"seriousnesshospitalization=1: {hosp_n:,} ({hosp_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"death OR hospitalization: {((sample['seriousnessdeath']==1)|(sample['seriousnesshospitalization']==1)).sum():,}")

serious=1: 104,896 (52.45%)
seriousnessdeath=1: 18,865 (9.43%)
seriousnesshospitalization=1: 38,124 (19.06%)
death OR hospitalization: 52,810

raw_evidence.label: What FAERS is and where this data comes from
raw_evidence.content: The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) is the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's central database for post-market drug safety reports. It collects voluntary reports from patients, caregivers, and clinicians via MedWatch, plus mandatory expedited reports from drug manufacturers. The system supports the FDA's post-market safety surveillance for drugs and therapeutic biologics. FAERS data is published quarterly and exposed via the OpenFDA Drug Adverse Event API at https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json. This blog uses a roughly chronological API-paginated sample of 200,000 reports with receivedate in 2024, drawn from a full-year universe of approximately 1.32 million reports.

raw_evidence.label: What FAERS is and where this data comes from
raw_evidence.content: The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) is the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's central database for post-market drug safety reports. It collects voluntary reports from patients, caregivers, and clinicians via MedWatch, plus mandatory expedited reports from drug manufacturers. The system supports the FDA's post-market safety surveillance for drugs and therapeutic biologics. FAERS data is published quarterly and exposed via the OpenFDA Drug Adverse Event API at https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json. This blog uses a roughly chronological API-paginated sample of 200,000 reports with receivedate in 2024, drawn from a full-year universe of approximately 1.32 million reports.

raw_evidence.label: How a FAERS report is structured
raw_evidence.content: Each FAERS record describes one adverse-event report. A report names one patient (age, sex, country), one or more drugs (each tagged as Suspect, Concomitant, or Interacting in the drugcharacterization field), and one or more reactions described as standardized MedDRA Preferred Terms. The report carries a single seriousness flag (`serious`: 1=serious, 2=not serious) and sub-flags for death and hospitalization. The reporter is classified by `reporttype` — 1=Spontaneous (the typical MedWatch submission), 2=Report from study, 3=Other, 4=Not available to sender. A single safetyreportid therefore explodes into many rows: one summary row, n_drugs drug rows, and n_reactions reaction rows.

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

Source: Ozempic, similar weight loss-diabetes drugs linked to 162 deaths, FDA reports (https://www.hmf-law.com/news/ozempic-wegovy-monjaro-162-deaths-fda/) Facts: Weight loss and diabetes drugs Ozempic, Mounjaro, and Wegovy linked to at least 162 deaths since 2018; 94 of the 162 deaths linked specifically to Ozempic and Wegovy Source: FDA Database Reveals High Number of Severe Adverse Events Involving Ozempic, Similar GLP1 Drugs (https://www.aboutlawsuits.com/ozempic-wegovy-mounjaro-lawsuit/severe-adverse-eve) Facts: Adverse-reaction reports linked to weight loss drugs increased about 40% in six months; 62,000 reported reactions to these medications in the U.S. since 2018 Source: Gastrointestinal Safety Assessment of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in the US: FAERS Analysis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11675942/) Facts: Among GLP-1 agonists, Trulicity (65,038), Byetta (48,898), and Mounjaro (30,283) had the highest cumulative adverse-event report counts; Semaglutide accounted for 26.1% of 31,439 GLP-1-related reports from Jan 2018 to Dec 2022

raw_evidence.label: The 2024 GLP-1 story: Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro flood the database
raw_evidence.content: The single largest story in FAERS during 2023–2024 is the explosion of reports about GLP-1 receptor agonists used for diabetes and weight loss — Ozempic and Wegovy (semaglutide, Novo Nordisk), Mounjaro and Zepbound (tirzepatide, Eli Lilly), and older entrants like Trulicity and Byetta. Press analyses of the FAERS dashboard in 2024 found that adverse-reaction reports linked to weight-loss drugs grew about 40% in six months, that roughly 46,000 of the 62,000 cumulative reports since 2018 had been filed after 2022, and that the FDA had recorded 162 deaths and roughly 10,000 'serious' reactions in the class. Tirzepatide reports outran semaglutide reports in 2023 and 2024 (about 15,000 vs 6,000 in 2023, and ~19,000 vs ~5,000 in 2024 per press accounts of the dashboard). The signature complaints are gastrointestinal — gastroparesis, ileus, intractable nausea — alongside ordinary 'Drug ineffective' filings. This is the cleanest example in the dataset of a real-world media-and-prescribing surge translating into a reporting surge.

raw_evidence.label: Suspect-role ranking: same leaders, sharper signal
raw_evidence.content: When the analysis is restricted to drugs marked as the *suspect* product (drugcharacterization = 1, meaning the reporter believes this drug caused the event), the field tightens and the ranking sharpens. Dupixent (14,916 suspect rows, 3.01% of all suspect-drug rows) is still #1 by a hair over Mounjaro (14,742, 2.98%). Acetaminophen drops from #8 to #21 because it is most often mentioned as a concomitant medication, not as the suspect. Aspirin disappears from the top 25 entirely. The suspect ranking is the more meaningful surveillance signal: it is roughly what FDA looks at when prioritizing safety signals.

raw_evidence.label: The 2024 GLP-1 story: Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro flood the database
raw_evidence.content: The single largest story in FAERS during 2023–2024 is the explosion of reports about GLP-1 receptor agonists used for diabetes and weight loss — Ozempic and Wegovy (semaglutide, Novo Nordisk), Mounjaro and Zepbound (tirzepatide, Eli Lilly), and older entrants like Trulicity and Byetta. Press analyses of the FAERS dashboard in 2024 found that adverse-reaction reports linked to weight-loss drugs grew about 40% in six months, that roughly 46,000 of the 62,000 cumulative reports since 2018 had been filed after 2022, and that the FDA had recorded 162 deaths and roughly 10,000 'serious' reactions in the class. Tirzepatide reports outran semaglutide reports in 2023 and 2024 (about 15,000 vs 6,000 in 2023, and ~19,000 vs ~5,000 in 2024 per press accounts of the dashboard). The signature complaints are gastrointestinal — gastroparesis, ileus, intractable nausea — alongside ordinary 'Drug ineffective' filings. This is the cleanest example in the dataset of a real-world media-and-prescribing surge translating into a reporting surge.

raw_evidence.label: Aspirin and acetaminophen are mostly bystanders, not suspects
raw_evidence.content: Drugs split sharply on whether they appear as the suspect or merely as concomitant medication. Dupixent (99.3% suspect), Mounjaro (98.9%), Xolair (99.1%), Repatha (99.0%), and Cabometyx (99.8%) are almost never reported as bystanders — when they show up, they are the drug under suspicion. By contrast, aspirin is the suspect in only 15.8% of its mentions (the other 83.0% are concomitant), and acetaminophen is 50/50. This is exactly what you would expect: people on cancer therapy or biologics are also on a daily aspirin or acetaminophen, but the reporter rarely blames the painkiller for an adverse event. The role mix is a useful diagnostic for whether a drug's headline count reflects a real safety signal or simply how common the prescription is.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: How often each top drug is the SUSPECT vs Concomitant ---
print("=== ana_08 ===")
top_names = top.index[:20]
rows = []
for n in top_names:
    sub = drugs[drugs["medicinalproduct_norm"] == n]
    total = len(sub)
    role_counts = sub["drugcharacterization"].value_counts()
    suspect = int(role_counts.get(1, 0))
    concomitant = int(role_counts.get(2, 0))
    interacting = int(role_counts.get(3, 0))
    other = total - suspect - concomitant - interacting
    rows.append((n, total, suspect, concomitant, interacting, other,
                 suspect/total*100, concomitant/total*100))
print("drug\ttotal\tsuspect\tconcom\tinteract\tother\tsuspect_pct\tconcom_pct")
for r in rows:
    print("\t".join(str(x) for x in r))

raw_evidence.label: Aspirin and acetaminophen are mostly bystanders, not suspects
raw_evidence.content: Drugs split sharply on whether they appear as the suspect or merely as concomitant medication. Dupixent (99.3% suspect), Mounjaro (98.9%), Xolair (99.1%), Repatha (99.0%), and Cabometyx (99.8%) are almost never reported as bystanders — when they show up, they are the drug under suspicion. By contrast, aspirin is the suspect in only 15.8% of its mentions (the other 83.0% are concomitant), and acetaminophen is 50/50. This is exactly what you would expect: people on cancer therapy or biologics are also on a daily aspirin or acetaminophen, but the reporter rarely blames the painkiller for an adverse event. The role mix is a useful diagnostic for whether a drug's headline count reflects a real safety signal or simply how common the prescription is.

print("=== ana_08 ===")
top_names = top.index[:20]
rows = []
for n in top_names:
    sub = drugs[drugs["medicinalproduct_norm"] == n]
    total = len(sub)
    role_counts = sub["drugcharacterization"].value_counts()
    suspect = int(role_counts.get(1, 0))
    concomitant = int(role_counts.get(2, 0))
    interacting = int(role_counts.get(3, 0))
    other = total - suspect - concomitant - interacting
    rows.append((n, total, suspect, concomitant, interacting, other,
                 suspect/total*100, concomitant/total*100))
print("drug\ttotal\tsuspect\tconcom\tinteract\tother\tsuspect_pct\tconcom_pct")
for r in rows:
    print("\t".join(str(x) for x in r))

The two are followed by Xolair (omalizumab for asthma) at 8,720 mentions and the workhorse cancer-clinic combo of methotrexate, prednisone, Repatha, and Cabometyx. Ozempic — the GLP-1 drug at the center of the 2024 weight-loss story — ranks twenty-first with 3,593 mentions; its sibling Zepbound, launched in November 2023, is right behind at 3,077. The headline story of the 2024 dataset is that Dupixent and the tirzepatide brands have crowded out the older immunology and oncology blockbusters that historically dominated FAERS.

Dulaglutide (Trulicity) is third at 2,060, followed by liraglutide (Victoza + Saxenda) at 455 and exenatide (Byetta + Bydureon) at just 195. The 10,056 unique reports involving any GLP-1 drug make up 5.03% of all FAERS reports in the sample. raw_evidence.label: The 2024 GLP-1 story: Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro flood the database
raw_evidence.content: The single largest story in FAERS during 2023–2024 is the explosion of reports about GLP-1 receptor agonists used for diabetes and weight loss — Ozempic and Wegovy (semaglutide, Novo Nordisk), Mounjaro and Zepbound (tirzepatide, Eli Lilly), and older entrants like Trulicity and Byetta. Press analyses of the FAERS dashboard in 2024 found that adverse-reaction reports linked to weight-loss drugs grew about 40% in six months, that roughly 46,000 of the 62,000 cumulative reports since 2018 had been filed after 2022, and that the FDA had recorded 162 deaths and roughly 10,000 'serious' reactions in the class. Tirzepatide reports outran semaglutide reports in 2023 and 2024 (about 15,000 vs 6,000 in 2023, and ~19,000 vs ~5,000 in 2024 per press accounts of the dashboard). The signature complaints are gastrointestinal — gastroparesis, ileus, intractable nausea — alongside ordinary 'Drug ineffective' filings. This is the cleanest example in the dataset of a real-world media-and-prescribing surge translating into a reporting surge.

raw_evidence.label: Tirzepatide outruns semaglutide 3.3 to 1 inside the GLP-1 class
raw_evidence.content: Pooled across all brand names, GLP-1 receptor agonists account for 26,170 drug rows — 3.37% of all drug appearances in the dataset. Within that class, tirzepatide (Mounjaro + Zepbound) is the dominant contributor at 18,035 rows, three-and-a-third times the 5,425 rows for semaglutide (Ozempic + Wegovy + Rybelsus). Dulaglutide (Trulicity) is third at 2,060, followed by liraglutide (Victoza + Saxenda) at 455 and exenatide (Byetta + Bydureon) at just 195. The 10,056 unique reports involving any GLP-1 drug make up 5.03% of all FAERS reports in the sample. The Mounjaro/Zepbound surge confirms — at the 2024 sampling moment — the press narrative that tirzepatide is generating disproportionately more reports than the older semaglutide products, despite a much shorter time on the market.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_09: GLP-1 receptor agonist family — every brand+generic ---
print("=== ana_09 ===")
GLP1_PATTERNS = {
    "semaglutide": ["OZEMPIC", "WEGOVY", "RYBELSUS", "SEMAGLUTIDE"],
    "tirzepatide": ["MOUNJARO", "ZEPBOUND", "TIRZEPATIDE"],
    "liraglutide": ["VICTOZA", "SAXENDA", "LIRAGLUTIDE"],
    "dulaglutide": ["TRULICITY", "DULAGLUTIDE"],
    "exenatide":   ["BYETTA", "BYDUREON", "EXENATIDE"],
    "lixisenatide": ["LYXUMIA", "ADLYXIN", "LIXISENATIDE"],
}
glp1_brand_to_generic = {}
for gen, brands in GLP1_PATTERNS.items():
    for b in brands:
        glp1_brand_to_generic[b] = gen

def glp1_match(name):
    if not isinstance(name, str):
        return None
    n = name.upper()
    for brand, gen in glp1_brand_to_generic.items():
        if brand in n:
            return gen
    return None

drugs["glp1_generic"] = drugs["medicinalproduct_norm"].apply(glp1_match)
glp1_rows = drugs[drugs["glp1_generic"].notna()]
print(f"GLP-1 drug rows: {len(glp1_rows):,} ({len(glp1_rows)/len(drugs)*100:.2f}% of all drug rows)")
print()
print("By generic:")
by_gen = glp1_rows["glp1_generic"].value_counts()
for g, n in by_gen.items():
    print(f"  {g}: {n:,}")

print()
print("Unique GLP-1 reports (safetyreportid):")
glp1_reports = glp1_rows["safetyreportid"].nunique()
total_reports = sample["safetyreportid"].nunique()
print(f"  GLP-1 reports: {glp1_reports:,} of {total_reports:,} ({glp1_reports/total_reports*100:.2f}%)")

raw_evidence.label: GLP-1 head-to-head: same class, very different report profiles
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to suspect-role reports for the eight major GLP-1 brand names, the brands split sharply on seriousness despite covering similar therapeutic territory. Mounjaro (3,159 suspect-reports, 11.0% serious, 0.70% death) and Zepbound (718 reports, 2.5% serious, 0.0% death) — both tirzepatide products — are remarkably mild compared with Ozempic (2,493 reports, 32.0% serious, 0.6% death) and Rybelsus (260, 35.8% serious, 1.2% death), both semaglutide. Wegovy (semaglutide for weight loss) sits in between at 25.0% serious. Saxenda (liraglutide for weight loss) is an outlier at 90.5% serious, but the sample is small (63 reports). Female share is high across all brands (60–82%); US share is even higher (80–98%); median age is younger for the weight-loss-indicated brands (Wegovy 47, Zepbound 49, Saxenda 45.5) than for the diabetes-indicated brands (Ozempic 63, Rybelsus 63, Trulicity 63).

# --- ana_32: Mounjaro vs Ozempic head-to-head (suspect role) ---
print("=== ana_32 ===")
brands = ["OZEMPIC", "WEGOVY", "RYBELSUS", "MOUNJARO", "ZEPBOUND", "TRULICITY", "VICTOZA", "SAXENDA"]
report_summary = sample.set_index("safetyreportid")[
    ["serious", "seriousnessdeath", "seriousnesshospitalization", "patient_sex", "patient_onset_age", "patient_onset_age_unit", "occurcountry"]
]
rows = []
for b in brands:
    sub = drugs[(drugs["m"] == b) & (drugs["drugcharacterization"] == 1)]
    reports = sub["safetyreportid"].unique()
    info = report_summary.reindex(reports).dropna(subset=["serious"])
    n = len(info)
    if n == 0: continue
    ser = int((info["serious"] == 1).sum())
    death = int((info["seriousnessdeath"] == 1).sum())
    hosp = int((info["seriousnesshospitalization"] == 1).sum())
    female = int((info["patient_sex"] == 2).sum())
    male = int((info["patient_sex"] == 1).sum())
    sex_known = female + male
    us = int((info["occurcountry"] == "US").sum())
    yrs = info[info["patient_onset_age_unit"] == 801]["patient_onset_age"]
    age_known = len(yrs)
    median_age = yrs.median() if len(yrs) else None
    rows.append((b, n, ser, death, hosp,
                 ser/n*100, death/n*100, hosp/n*100,
                 female, male, female/sex_known*100 if sex_known else 0,
                 us, us/n*100,
                 age_known, median_age))
print("brand\treports\tserious\tdeath\thosp\tser%\tdth%\thsp%\tfemale\tmale\tfemale%\tUS\tUS%\tage_known\tmed_age")
for r in rows:
    print("\t".join(f"{x:.2f}" if isinstance(x, float) else str(x) for x in r))

raw_evidence.label: GLP-1 head-to-head: same class, very different report profiles
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to suspect-role reports for the eight major GLP-1 brand names, the brands split sharply on seriousness despite covering similar therapeutic territory. Mounjaro (3,159 suspect-reports, 11.0% serious, 0.70% death) and Zepbound (718 reports, 2.5% serious, 0.0% death) — both tirzepatide products — are remarkably mild compared with Ozempic (2,493 reports, 32.0% serious, 0.6% death) and Rybelsus (260, 35.8% serious, 1.2% death), both semaglutide. Wegovy (semaglutide for weight loss) sits in between at 25.0% serious. Saxenda (liraglutide for weight loss) is an outlier at 90.5% serious, but the sample is small (63 reports). Female share is high across all brands (60–82%); US share is even higher (80–98%); median age is younger for the weight-loss-indicated brands (Wegovy 47, Zepbound 49, Saxenda 45.5) than for the diabetes-indicated brands (Ozempic 63, Rybelsus 63, Trulicity 63).

# --- ana_32: Mounjaro vs Ozempic head-to-head (suspect role) ---
print("=== ana_32 ===")
brands = ["OZEMPIC", "WEGOVY", "RYBELSUS", "MOUNJARO", "ZEPBOUND", "TRULICITY", "VICTOZA", "SAXENDA"]
report_summary = sample.set_index("safetyreportid")[
    ["serious", "seriousnessdeath", "seriousnesshospitalization", "patient_sex", "patient_onset_age", "patient_onset_age_unit", "occurcountry"]
]
rows = []
for b in brands:
    sub = drugs[(drugs["m"] == b) & (drugs["drugcharacterization"] == 1)]
    reports = sub["safetyreportid"].unique()
    info = report_summary.reindex(reports).dropna(subset=["serious"])
    n = len(info)
    if n == 0: continue
    ser = int((info["serious"] == 1).sum())
    death = int((info["seriousnessdeath"] == 1).sum())
    hosp = int((info["seriousnesshospitalization"] == 1).sum())
    female = int((info["patient_sex"] == 2).sum())
    male = int((info["patient_sex"] == 1).sum())
    sex_known = female + male
    us = int((info["occurcountry"] == "US").sum())
    yrs = info[info["patient_onset_age_unit"] == 801]["patient_onset_age"]
    age_known = len(yrs)
    median_age = yrs.median() if len(yrs) else None
    rows.append((b, n, ser, death, hosp,
                 ser/n*100, death/n*100, hosp/n*100,
                 female, male, female/sex_known*100 if sex_known else 0,
                 us, us/n*100,
                 age_known, median_age))
print("brand\treports\tserious\tdeath\thosp\tser%\tdth%\thsp%\tfemale\tmale\tfemale%\tUS\tUS%\tage_known\tmed_age")
for r in rows:
    print("\t".join(f"{x:.2f}" if isinstance(x, float) else str(x) for x in r))

raw_evidence.label: Mounjaro's complaints are about the pen; Ozempic's are about the body
raw_evidence.content: The top reactions for the two leading GLP-1 brands look almost like reports from different drugs. Mounjaro's top complaints are dosing-and-device events: 'Incorrect dose administered' (21.7% of Mounjaro reports), 'Injection site pain' (14.5%), 'Off label use' (12.5%), 'Extra dose administered' (7.7%), 'Injection site haemorrhage' (6.9%). Only at rank 4 does a biological symptom appear ('Nausea', 9.9%). Ozempic's profile is the inverse: 'Nausea' is #1 (16.2%), followed by 'Off label use' (10.1%), 'Vomiting' (9.3%), 'Diarrhoea' (9.2%), 'Constipation' (7.6%), and 'Decreased appetite' (6.8%). Most plausibly, the two drugs use different pen-injector devices and have different reporter communities — Mounjaro's pen seems to invite more device-handling complaints, while Ozempic's older clinical-trial reporting habits leak through into more symptom-style reports.

raw_evidence.label: Mounjaro's complaints are about the pen; Ozempic's are about the body
raw_evidence.content: The top reactions for the two leading GLP-1 brands look almost like reports from different drugs. Mounjaro's top complaints are dosing-and-device events: 'Incorrect dose administered' (21.7% of Mounjaro reports), 'Injection site pain' (14.5%), 'Off label use' (12.5%), 'Extra dose administered' (7.7%), 'Injection site haemorrhage' (6.9%). Only at rank 4 does a biological symptom appear ('Nausea', 9.9%). Ozempic's profile is the inverse: 'Nausea' is #1 (16.2%), followed by 'Off label use' (10.1%), 'Vomiting' (9.3%), 'Diarrhoea' (9.2%), 'Constipation' (7.6%), and 'Decreased appetite' (6.8%). Most plausibly, the two drugs use different pen-injector devices and have different reporter communities — Mounjaro's pen seems to invite more device-handling complaints, while Ozempic's older clinical-trial reporting habits leak through into more symptom-style reports.

raw_evidence.label: The 2024 GLP-1 story: Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro flood the database
raw_evidence.content: The single largest story in FAERS during 2023–2024 is the explosion of reports about GLP-1 receptor agonists used for diabetes and weight loss — Ozempic and Wegovy (semaglutide, Novo Nordisk), Mounjaro and Zepbound (tirzepatide, Eli Lilly), and older entrants like Trulicity and Byetta. Press analyses of the FAERS dashboard in 2024 found that adverse-reaction reports linked to weight-loss drugs grew about 40% in six months, that roughly 46,000 of the 62,000 cumulative reports since 2018 had been filed after 2022, and that the FDA had recorded 162 deaths and roughly 10,000 'serious' reactions in the class. Tirzepatide reports outran semaglutide reports in 2023 and 2024 (about 15,000 vs 6,000 in 2023, and ~19,000 vs ~5,000 in 2024 per press accounts of the dashboard). The signature complaints are gastrointestinal — gastroparesis, ileus, intractable nausea — alongside ordinary 'Drug ineffective' filings. This is the cleanest example in the dataset of a real-world media-and-prescribing surge translating into a reporting surge.

raw_evidence.label: What GLP-1 reports actually say: hunger, gastroparesis, dose mishaps
raw_evidence.content: Computing each reaction's representation rate inside GLP-1 reports versus the whole dataset reveals a class signature. The most over-represented reactions are 'Allodynia' (21.2x more common in GLP-1 reports than in the dataset average), 'Weight loss poor' (18.5x — patients reporting the drug isn't taking enough weight off), 'Impaired gastric emptying' (14.8x — the gastroparesis signal that became a 2024 news story), 'Eructation' (13.9x — burping), 'Accidental underdose' (13.6x), 'Hunger' (12.4x), 'Increased appetite' (11.1x), 'Pancreatitis' (8.4x — a long-known GLP-1 risk), 'Incorrect dose administered' (8.2x), and 'Injection site pain' (5.4x). The paradox at the heart of the class is on display: both 'Weight loss poor' AND 'Increased appetite' show extreme lift, alongside 'Hunger' — meaning a non-trivial subset of reports are from patients complaining the drug isn't working as advertised.

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

raw_evidence.label: The death-rate hotspots are overdose drugs, not weight-loss drugs
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to drugs with at least 200 suspect-reports, the highest death rates belong to drugs primarily implicated in overdose: methamphetamine (93.5% of its suspect-reports involve a death), alcohol (89.4%), fentanyl (71.9%), diphenhydramine (70.9%), trazodone (69.1%), cocaine (66.1%), and oxycodone (57.9%). These are not signals that the drugs are killing properly-prescribed patients — they are reports filed because someone died with that substance present. Alendronic acid (Fosamax) appears in this group too, but for a different reason: it is reported in atypical-fracture and osteonecrosis cases that have high mortality among elderly patients. Notably absent from the top-30 death-rate list: any GLP-1 drug.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_20: Death-rate hot drugs (require >= 200 suspect-reports to filter noise) ---
print("=== ana_20 ===")
# Build for ALL drugs with >= 200 suspect-reports
agg = (sus.groupby("m")["safetyreportid"].nunique()
       .reset_index().rename(columns={"safetyreportid": "n_reports"}))
agg = agg[agg["n_reports"] >= 200].copy()
# For each: join to seriousness
def stats_for(name):
    reports = sus[sus["m"] == name]["safetyreportid"].unique()
    sub = report_serious.reindex(reports).dropna(subset=["serious"])
    n = len(sub)
    if n == 0: return (0, 0, 0)
    return (n, int((sub["seriousnessdeath"] == 1).sum()),
            int((sub["seriousnesshospitalization"] == 1).sum()))
stats = agg["m"].apply(stats_for)
agg["n"] = stats.apply(lambda x: x[0])
agg["death"] = stats.apply(lambda x: x[1])
agg["hosp"]  = stats.apply(lambda x: x[2])
agg["death_pct"] = agg["death"] / agg["n"] * 100
agg["hosp_pct"]  = agg["hosp"]  / agg["n"] * 100
print("TOP-30 by death_pct (>=200 reports):")
print(agg.sort_values("death_pct", ascending=False).head(30)[
    ["m", "n_reports", "death", "death_pct", "hosp", "hosp_pct"]
].to_string(index=False))

print()
print("TOP-30 by hosp_pct (>=200 reports):")
print(agg.sort_values("hosp_pct", ascending=False).head(30)[
    ["m", "n_reports", "death", "death_pct", "hosp", "hosp_pct"]
].to_string(index=False))

These are not signals that the drugs are killing properly-prescribed patients — they are reports filed because someone died with that substance present. Alendronic acid (Fosamax) appears in this group too, but for a different reason: it is reported in atypical-fracture and osteonecrosis cases that have high mortality among elderly patients. Notably absent from the top-30 death-rate list: any GLP-1 drug.

       .reset_index().rename(columns={"safetyreportid": "n_reports"}))

    sub = report_serious.reindex(reports).dropna(subset=["serious"])
    n = len(sub)

print("TOP-30 by death_pct (>=200 reports):")

raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. raw_evidence.label: What people die of in FAERS: cardiac arrest, suicide, sepsis
raw_evidence.content: Within the 39,213 reaction rows tagged with the Fatal outcome code, the MedDRA term 'Death' itself accounts for 21.6% — meaning many reports list 'Death' as both the reaction and the outcome rather than naming a specific cause. 'Completed suicide' is the most common identifiable cause at 4.1% (1,602 fatal rows), followed by 'Toxicity to various agents' (2.7%), 'Drug abuse' (2.2%), 'Cardio-respiratory arrest' (1.2%), 'Pneumonia' (0.9%), and 'Cardiac arrest' (0.8%). Notably, 'Drug ineffective' itself appears 304 times with a fatal outcome — these are cases where a drug failed to prevent a fatal outcome it was prescribed to treat (e.g. cancer therapy in metastatic disease).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_16: Fatal-outcome reactions — which PTs are most often tagged Fatal (code 5) ---
print("=== ana_16 ===")
fatal = reactions[reactions["reactionoutcome"] == 5]
top_fatal = fatal["reactionmeddrapt"].value_counts().head(30)
total_fatal_rows = len(fatal)
print(f"total fatal-outcome reaction rows: {total_fatal_rows:,}")
for pt, n in top_fatal.items():
    print(f"{pt}\t{n:,}\t{n/total_fatal_rows*100:.2f}%")

sources.title: Existence of Notoriety Bias in FDA Adverse Event Reporting System Database
facts: Notoriety bias occurs where media coverage or regulatory warnings increase the likelihood of specific adverse event reporting

raw_evidence.label: The death-rate hotspots are overdose drugs, not weight-loss drugs
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to drugs with at least 200 suspect-reports, the highest death rates belong to drugs primarily implicated in overdose: methamphetamine (93.5% of its suspect-reports involve a death), alcohol (89.4%), fentanyl (71.9%), diphenhydramine (70.9%), trazodone (69.1%), cocaine (66.1%), and oxycodone (57.9%). These are not signals that the drugs are killing properly-prescribed patients — they are reports filed because someone died with that substance present. Alendronic acid (Fosamax) appears in this group too, but for a different reason: it is reported in atypical-fracture and osteonecrosis cases that have high mortality among elderly patients. Notably absent from the top-30 death-rate list: any GLP-1 drug.

agg = (sus.groupby("m")["safetyreportid"].nunique()
       .reset_index().rename(columns={"safetyreportid": "n_reports"}))
agg = agg[agg["n_reports"] >= 200].copy()
# For each: join to seriousness
def stats_for(name):
    reports = sus[sus["m"] == name]["safetyreportid"].unique()
    sub = report_serious.reindex(reports).dropna(subset=["serious"])

agg["death"] = stats.apply(lambda x: x[1])

raw_evidence.label: Who actually files FAERS reports — and where they live
raw_evidence.content: Although FAERS is a U.S. system, anyone in the world can submit a report and manufacturers must forward reports from any country where their drug is sold. In practice the U.S. dominates the submissions: it is both the country where the events most often occur (`occurcountry`) and the country of the reporter (`primarysourcecountry`). But the long tail includes many European countries, Japan, and major manufacturing hubs. The skew matters because reporting culture differs by country — Germany and Japan, for instance, push manufacturer-mediated reports through national systems that then forward to FAERS, while U.S. reports include a much larger proportion of direct consumer submissions through MedWatch. Country comparisons therefore say as much about reporting infrastructure as they do about drug safety.

raw_evidence.label: FAERS reports skew strongly female: 1.47 women per man
raw_evidence.content: Among reports with a known patient sex, 99,513 (59.5% of sex-known) are female and 67,785 (40.5%) are male — a 1.47:1 ratio. Including the 15.9% of reports with missing sex and the 0.4% explicitly coded Unknown, the absolute counts are: 49.8% female, 33.9% male, 0.4% unknown, 15.9% missing. The female skew is consistent with decades of pharmacovigilance literature: women are prescribed more drugs on average, are more likely to report symptoms to clinicians, and are over-represented in the conditions whose drugs file the most reports (autoimmune disease, depression, osteoporosis, weight-loss). It is also a known source of bias — the FAERS picture of any given drug is colored by who is filing reports about it, not just who is taking it.

raw_evidence.label: Daily volume reveals a hard weekday/weekend bureaucracy
raw_evidence.content: Across the 54-day window, daily report counts oscillate wildly: weekdays average around 4,000–6,800 reports per day, while Saturdays and Sundays plummet to 400–900. January 6 (a Saturday) received 668 reports, January 7 (Sunday) received 464 — both less than 10% of the surrounding Friday's 6,621. The pattern repeats every weekend across both January and February. This is not because adverse events stop happening on weekends — it is because the reporting channels (manufacturer pharmacovigilance teams, FDA intake systems, hospital safety officers) work weekday shifts and queue weekend reports for Monday processing.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_29: Daily report volume across the 54-day window ---
print("=== ana_29 ===")
daily = sample.groupby(sample["dt"].dt.date).size().reset_index(name="n_reports")
daily.columns = ["date", "n_reports"]
print(daily.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: Weekdays carry 93% of all reports
raw_evidence.content: Aggregating by day-of-week across the eight weeks of the window, weekdays total 186,244 reports (93.1% of all 200,000) while Saturdays and Sundays combined total just 13,756 (6.9%). The most active day is Wednesday (39,720 reports), the least active is Saturday (5,561). The asymmetry — Sunday (8,195) is higher than Saturday (5,561) — likely reflects manufacturers queuing weekend reports for early-Monday submission, with some of those submissions being timestamped to Sunday because of overnight batch processing.

print(f"weekend total: {dow[5:].sum():,}")

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

raw_evidence.label: FAERS-driven safety signals in late 2024
raw_evidence.content: FDA publishes a quarterly list of 'Potential Signals of Serious Risks/New Safety Information' that were first surfaced by FAERS reports. The list for October–December 2024 includes drugs and signals such as ofatumumab (mood-disorder reports), trazodone (serotonin syndrome and drug interactions), and several others. The existence of this list is the practical answer to 'so what does FAERS actually do?': clusters of reports inside this database — sometimes only a few dozen — trigger formal FDA action, including label changes, dose warnings, and Drug Safety Communications. The fact that a drug appears on a quarterly signal list does not establish causation; it only means FDA decided the pattern was worth a closer look.

raw_evidence.label: 52% of reports are tagged 'serious'; 9% record a death
raw_evidence.content: The serious flag is on in 104,896 of 200,000 reports (52.5%). Of those, 18,865 reports (9.4% of all 200,000) carry the seriousnessdeath sub-flag, and 38,124 (19.1%) carry the seriousnesshospitalization sub-flag. The 'serious' rate is much higher than naive expectation because serious events are far more likely to be reported in the first place — a mild headache rarely makes it into FAERS, but a hospitalization almost always does. The 9.4% death rate is therefore not 'how often this drug kills' but 'what share of reports involve a death'.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_18: Overall seriousness rates ---
print("=== ana_18 ===")
N = len(sample)
serious_n = (sample["serious"] == 1).sum()
notser_n  = (sample["serious"] == 2).sum()
death_n   = (sample["seriousnessdeath"] == 1).sum()
hosp_n    = (sample["seriousnesshospitalization"] == 1).sum()
print(f"total reports: {N:,}")
print(f"serious=1: {serious_n:,} ({serious_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"serious=2 (not serious): {notser_n:,} ({notser_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"seriousnessdeath=1: {death_n:,} ({death_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"seriousnesshospitalization=1: {hosp_n:,} ({hosp_n/N*100:.2f}%)")
print(f"death OR hospitalization: {((sample['seriousnessdeath']==1)|(sample['seriousnesshospitalization']==1)).sum():,}")
raw_evidence.output:
serious=1: 104,896 (52.45%)
seriousnessdeath=1: 18,865 (9.43%)
seriousnesshospitalization=1: 38,124 (19.06%)
death OR hospitalization: 52,810

raw_evidence.label: 52% of reports are tagged 'serious'; 9% record a death
raw_evidence.content: The serious flag is on in 104,896 of 200,000 reports (52.5%). Of those, 18,865 reports (9.4% of all 200,000) carry the seriousnessdeath sub-flag, and 38,124 (19.1%) carry the seriousnesshospitalization sub-flag. The 'serious' rate is much higher than naive expectation because serious events are far more likely to be reported in the first place — a mild headache rarely makes it into FAERS, but a hospitalization almost always does. The 9.4% death rate is therefore not 'how often this drug kills' but 'what share of reports involve a death'.

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

raw_evidence.label: Why FAERS reports are not the same as adverse-event rates
raw_evidence.content: FAERS is a passive surveillance system. Reporting is voluntary for patients and clinicians, and even the manufacturer-mandated reports are filtered through whoever notices and writes them up. The result is well-known structural distortions: most adverse drug reactions are never reported at all; serious events are reported more often than mild ones; and 'notoriety bias' inflates counts for any drug that has recently been in the news or under regulatory warning. Crucially, FAERS has no denominator — it does not know how many patients took each drug — so a raw report count cannot be converted into a per-patient risk. FDA itself states that FAERS is most valuable for generating hypotheses about potential safety signals, which must then be confirmed by controlled studies. Every chart in this blog should be read as 'reports submitted', not 'events that happened in the world'.

raw_evidence.label: FAERS-driven safety signals in late 2024
raw_evidence.content: FDA publishes a quarterly list of 'Potential Signals of Serious Risks/New Safety Information' that were first surfaced by FAERS reports. The list for October–December 2024 includes drugs and signals such as ofatumumab (mood-disorder reports), trazodone (serotonin syndrome and drug interactions), and several others. The existence of this list is the practical answer to 'so what does FAERS actually do?': clusters of reports inside this database — sometimes only a few dozen — trigger formal FDA action, including label changes, dose warnings, and Drug Safety Communications. The fact that a drug appears on a quarterly signal list does not establish causation; it only means FDA decided the pattern was worth a closer look.
